notes:
1. Meaning of Fundamental Duties

  • Fundamental Duties are constitutional civic obligations addressed to citizens.

They express the responsibilities that citizens owe to:

  • Constitutional order.
  • Society.
  • Nation.
  • They encourage responsible conduct necessary for constitutional democracy.

They promote:

  • Constitutional discipline.
  • Patriotism.
  • Social responsibility.
  • Environmental awareness.
  • Scientific outlook.
  • Public spirit.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Duties → Constitutional Responsibilities of Citizens

2. Importance of Fundamental Duties

Fundamental Duties encourage citizens to:

  • Respect constitutional institutions.
  • Exercise freedoms responsibly.
  • Promote social harmony.
  • Protect common resources.
  • Participate in nation-building.
  • Balance individual interests with collective welfare.
  • Constitutional democracy requires both protected rights and responsible citizenship.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rights → Protect Freedom

Duties → Promote Responsible Citizenship

3. Constitutional Significance

  • Fundamental Duties are expressly included in the Constitution.
  • They therefore possess greater constitutional significance than ordinary moral advice.

Although generally non-justiciable, they influence:

  • Legislation.
  • Public policy.
  • Civic education.
  • Judicial interpretation.
  • Environmental regulation.
  • Protection of national symbols.

4. Fundamental Duties Were Not in the Original Constitution

  • The Constitution came into force in 1950 without a separate list of Fundamental Duties.

The original Constitution contained:

  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Directive Principles.
  • A separate constitutional list of citizen duties was added only in 1976.
📌 Must-Memorise

Original Constitution, 1950 → No Fundamental Duties

5. Historical Development

Important stages were:

  • 1950 → No separate constitutional list of Fundamental Duties.
  • 1976 → Swaran Singh Committee recommended inclusion.
  • 1976 → 42nd Constitutional Amendment inserted ten duties.
  • 1998 → J.S. Verma Committee examined existing laws implementing duty-related values.
  • 2002 → 86th Constitutional Amendment added the eleventh duty.
📌 Ultra-Short Memory

1950 → None

1976 → 10 Duties

1998 → Verma Committee

2002 → 11th Duty

6. Swaran Singh Committee, 1976

  • The Government appointed the Swaran Singh Committee in 1976.
  • Its central recommendation was to incorporate Fundamental Duties into the Constitution.

The accepted result was the insertion of:

  • Part IVA.
  • Article 51A.
  • Ten Fundamental Duties.
  • The Committee also proposed stronger legal consequences for non-compliance.
  • Not all of those additional recommendations were incorporated into the Constitution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Swaran Singh Committee → 1976 → Recommended Fundamental Duties

7. Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976

  • The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act inserted Fundamental Duties.

It added:

  • Part IVA.
  • Article 51A.
  • Ten Fundamental Duties.
  • All the first ten duties were inserted together through this Amendment.
📌 Must-Memorise

42nd Amendment, 1976 → Part IVA + Article 51A + 10 Duties

8. J.S. Verma Committee, 1998

  • The Justice J.S. Verma Committee examined the practical implementation of Fundamental Duties.
  • It identified existing laws that already gave legal effect to several duty-related values.

The Committee examined laws connected with:

  • National honour.
  • Public property.
  • Environment.
  • Social harmony.
  • Women's dignity.
  • Education.
  • National integrity.
📌 Must-Memorise

J.S. Verma Committee → 1998 → Existing Laws Enforcing Duty-Related Values

9. Swaran Singh Committee vs Verma Committee

Swaran Singh Committee:

  • 1976.
  • Recommended constitutional inclusion.
  • Led to the 42nd Amendment.

J.S. Verma Committee:

  • 1998.
  • Examined practical legal enforcement.
  • Identified existing implementing statutes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Swaran Singh → Addition of Duties

Verma → Implementation of Duties

10. Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002

  • The 86th Constitutional Amendment added Article 51A(k).
  • It created an educational duty for parents or guardians.

The total number of Fundamental Duties therefore increased:

  • From 10.
  • To 11.

The same Amendment also:

  • Inserted Article 21A.
  • Modified Article 45.
📌 Must-Memorise

86th Amendment, 2002 → 11th Duty → Article 51A(k)

11. Part IVA

  • Fundamental Duties are contained in Part IVA of the Constitution.

Part IVA contains only one Article:

  • Article 51A.
  • Part IVA was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

It is located between:

  • Part IV — Directive Principles.
  • Part V — The Union.
📌 Must-Memorise

Part IVA → Fundamental Duties

Only Article → 51A

12. Duties Apply Only to Citizens

  • Article 51A begins with the constitutional idea that it shall be the duty of every citizen of India.
  • Therefore Fundamental Duties apply constitutionally to Indian citizens.

They do not directly apply as Fundamental Duties to:

  • Foreigners.
  • Companies.
  • Artificial legal persons.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Fundamental Duties → Citizens Only

13. Original and Present Number

Originally in 1976:

  • 10 Fundamental Duties.

At present:

  • 11 Fundamental Duties.
  • The first ten were inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
  • Only Article 51A(k) was added later by the 86th Amendment.
📌 Must-Memorise

1976 → 10

2002 → 11

14. Non-Justiciable Nature

  • Fundamental Duties are generally non-justiciable.
  • Article 51A does not provide a direct constitutional remedy for their enforcement.

It does not itself prescribe:

  • Punishment.
  • Compensation.
  • Disqualification.
  • Direct judicial remedy.
  • There is no Article 32-type remedy for enforcing every Fundamental Duty.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Duties → Generally Non-Justiciable

15. Non-Justiciable Does Not Mean Unimportant

Fundamental Duties may still influence:

  • Judicial reasoning.
  • Legislation.
  • Public policy.
  • School curricula.
  • Environmental protection.
  • Civic campaigns.
  • National-symbol protection.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Non-Justiciable ≠ Legally Meaningless

16. No Direct Punishment under Article 51A

  • A person cannot ordinarily be punished merely because a Fundamental Duty has not been performed.

Punishment requires:

  • A valid law.
  • A defined legal obligation.
  • A prescribed penalty.
  • Due legal procedure.
  • Article 51A itself does not create criminal offences.
📌 Must-Memorise

Violation of Duty Alone → No Automatic Punishment

17. Legislative Enforcement

  • Parliament and State Legislatures may enact laws connected with Fundamental Duties where they possess legislative competence.
  • Such laws may create enforceable obligations and penalties.
  • In that situation, punishment arises from the implementing legislation rather than directly from Article 51A.

18. Positive and Negative Elements

Some duties require positive action:

  • Protect environment.
  • Develop scientific temper.
  • Promote harmony.
  • Preserve culture.
  • Strive for excellence.

Some duties also require restraint:

  • Abjure violence.
  • Safeguard public property.
  • Renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity.

19. Broad Constitutional Language

Article 51A uses expressions such as:

  • Cherish.
  • Uphold.
  • Promote.
  • Preserve.
  • Develop.
  • Strive.
  • These expressions provide broad constitutional guidance rather than detailed criminal-law commands.

20. Moral and Constitutional Character

Fundamental Duties possess both dimensions.

Moral dimension:

  • Encourages voluntary civic responsibility.
  • Operates even without punishment.
  • Depends significantly on citizen conduct.

Constitutional dimension:

  • Expressly included in Constitution.
  • Guides legislation.
  • Influences policy.
  • Assists judicial interpretation.

21. Individual and Collective Dimensions

Individual conduct includes:

  • Respecting Constitution.
  • Protecting public property.
  • Developing scientific temper.

Collective responsibility includes:

  • Promoting harmony.
  • Preserving composite culture.
  • Protecting environment.
  • Striving for national excellence.

22. Article 51A(a) — Constitution and National Symbols

Every citizen has a duty to:

  • Abide by the Constitution.
  • Respect its ideals.
  • Respect constitutional institutions.
  • Respect the National Flag.
  • Respect the National Anthem.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(a) → Constitution + Institutions + Flag + Anthem

23. Meaning of Constitutional Respect

  • Loyalty is owed to the constitutional order rather than to any particular political party or ruler.

Constitutional institutions include bodies and offices such as:

  • Parliament.
  • Judiciary.
  • Election Commission.
  • Constitutional offices.

Respect for the Constitution does not prohibit:

  • Lawful criticism.
  • Democratic disagreement.
  • Peaceful constitutional reform.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Respect Constitution ≠ Ban on Lawful Criticism

24. Article 51A(b) — Freedom Struggle Ideals

Every citizen has a duty to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired India's freedom struggle.

Important ideals include:

  • Liberty.
  • Equality.
  • Sacrifice.
  • Non-violence.
  • National unity.
  • Social reform.
  • Democratic participation.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(b) → Noble Ideals of Freedom Struggle

25. Freedom Struggle Duty

  • Article 51A(b) seeks preservation of constitutional values arising from the national movement.
  • It does not require uncritical acceptance of every historical political position.
  • The focus is on enduring ideals associated with freedom and democratic nation-building.

26. Article 51A(c) — Sovereignty, Unity and Integrity

Every citizen must uphold and protect:

  • Sovereignty of India.
  • Unity of India.
  • Integrity of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(c) → Sovereignty + Unity + Integrity

27. Meaning of Sovereignty, Unity and Integrity

Sovereignty:

  • India's independent authority in internal and external affairs.

Unity:

  • Common constitutional and political belonging.

Integrity:

  • Territorial and national wholeness.
  • The duty opposes secession, violent disintegration and destruction of constitutional unity.
  • Lawful regional identity and constitutional democratic demands remain permissible.

28. Article 51A(d) — Defence and National Service

Every citizen must:

  • Defend the country.
  • Render national service when called upon according to law.

This may relate to circumstances such as:

  • War.
  • National emergency.
  • Disaster.
  • Civil defence.
  • Other legally authorised national needs.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(d) → Defend Country + National Service

29. No Automatic Compulsory Military Service

  • Article 51A(d) does not by itself establish universal compulsory military service.
  • National service arises when citizens are lawfully called upon under an applicable legal framework.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 51A(d) ≠ Automatic Compulsory Military Service

30. Article 51A(e) — Harmony and Women's Dignity

Every citizen must:

  • Promote harmony.
  • Promote common brotherhood.

Rise above:

  • Religious differences.
  • Linguistic differences.
  • Regional differences.
  • Sectional differences.
  • Renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(e) → Harmony + Brotherhood + Dignity of Women

31. Women's Dignity

Article 51A(e) supports rejection of:

  • Violence.
  • Humiliation.
  • Exploitation.
  • Discrimination.
  • Practices degrading women.

It connects civic duty with:

  • Gender equality.
  • Human dignity.
  • Social harmony.

32. Article 51A(f) — Composite Culture

Every citizen has a duty to value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture.

📌 Must-Memorise

51A(f) → Composite Culture

33. Meaning of Composite Culture

The duty may involve preservation of:

  • Monuments.
  • Literature.
  • Music.
  • Dance.
  • Crafts.
  • Languages.
  • Folk traditions.
  • Cultural interaction among different regions and communities.
  • Composite culture does not mean cultural uniformity.
  • It reflects unity through diversity.

34. Article 51A(g) — Environment

Every citizen must:

  • Protect the natural environment.
  • Improve the natural environment.
  • Show compassion for living creatures.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(g) → Environment + Compassion for Living Creatures

35. Environmental Scope

Article 51A(g) includes responsibility relating to:

  • Forests.
  • Lakes.
  • Rivers.
  • Wildlife.
  • Pollution prevention.
  • Water conservation.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Sustainable practices.

36. Environment Constitutional Link

Environmental protection connects:

  • Article 21 → Judicially developed environmental dimension.
  • Article 48A → State responsibility.
  • Article 51A(g) → Citizen responsibility.
📌 Must-Memorise

21 → Environmental Right Dimension

48A → State Duty

51A(g) → Citizen Duty

37. Article 51A(h) — Scientific Temper

Every citizen has a duty to develop:

  • Scientific temper.
  • Humanism.
  • Spirit of inquiry.
  • Spirit of reform.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(h) → Scientific Temper + Humanism + Inquiry + Reform

38. Meaning of Scientific Temper

Scientific temper encourages citizens to:

  • Use evidence-based reasoning.
  • Question assumptions.
  • Test claims.
  • Remain open to new knowledge.
  • Respect human dignity.
  • Challenge harmful customs.
  • Support positive social reform.

39. Article 51A(i) — Public Property and Violence

Every citizen must:

  • Safeguard public property.
  • Abjure violence.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(i) → Public Property + No Violence

40. Meaning of Public Property

Public property may include:

  • Government buildings.
  • Public transport.
  • Schools.
  • Hospitals.
  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Public utilities.

Citizens should protect such property even during:

  • Protests.
  • Strikes.
  • Political movements.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Lawful Protest ≠ Right to Damage Public Property

41. Article 51A(j) — Excellence

Every citizen must strive towards excellence in all spheres of:

  • Individual activity.
  • Collective activity.

Examples include:

  • Education.
  • Science.
  • Sports.
  • Administration.
  • Arts.
  • Industry.
  • Public service.
  • Social conduct.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(j) → Strive for Excellence

42. Purpose of Excellence

  • Article 51A(j) encourages continuous improvement.

Excellence should contribute to:

  • Individual development.
  • Institutional improvement.
  • National progress.
  • The duty operates according to ability and opportunity.

43. Article 51A(k) — Educational Opportunity

  • A parent or guardian has a duty to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward aged 6–14 years.
  • Article 51A(k) was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(k) → Parent/Guardian → Education → 6–14 Years

44. Education Constitutional Link

Elementary education connects:

  • Article 21A → State obligation.
  • Article 45 → Early childhood constitutional policy.
  • Article 51A(k) → Parent or guardian responsibility.
📌 Ultra-Short Memory

State → 21A

Below 6 → 45

Parent/Guardian 6–14 → 51A(k)

45. Unique Feature of Article 51A(k)

Article 51A(k) is the only Fundamental Duty specifically addressed to:

  • Parents.
  • Guardians.
  • The other duties are generally addressed to every citizen.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Only Parent/Guardian-Specific Duty → Article 51A(k)

47. Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971

  • This law supports values associated with Article 51A(a).

It protects:

  • Constitution.
  • National Flag.
  • National Anthem.
  • It penalises specified intentional insult or disrespect.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Honour Act, 1971 → Article 51A(a)

48. Flag Code of India, 2002

The Flag Code consolidates conventions and instructions relating to:

  • Display of National Flag.
  • Position of honour.
  • Private use.
  • Prevention of disrespect.
  • It supports the constitutional duty under Article 51A(a).

49. Emblems and Names Act, 1950

The Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 restricts improper commercial or professional use of specified:

  • National emblems.
  • Official names.
  • Government symbols.

50. Representation of the People Act, 1951

  • The Act contains electoral offences and corrupt-practice provisions.
  • It includes restrictions on specified divisive electoral appeals.

These provisions support constitutional values concerning:

  • Unity.
  • Electoral integrity.
  • Social harmony.

51. Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967

UAPA addresses specified unlawful activities affecting:

  • Sovereignty.
  • Integrity.
  • Security.
  • It is connected with values reflected in Article 51A(c).
  • Restrictions under such legislation must independently comply with constitutional requirements.

52. Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955

  • The Protection of Civil Rights Act punishes enforcement of disabilities arising from untouchability.

It supports constitutional values concerning:

  • Equality.
  • Harmony.
  • Human dignity.

53. SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act, 1989

The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 protects persons against specified:

  • Caste-based atrocities.
  • Humiliating practices.
  • It supports equal citizenship and dignity.

54. Laws Supporting Women's Dignity

Important laws connected with the values of Article 51A(e) include:

  • Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
  • Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
  • Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013.
📌 Must-Memorise

51A(e) → Harmony + Women's Dignity

The Act prohibits:

  • Giving dowry.
  • Taking dowry.
  • Demanding dowry.
  • It supports the constitutional objective of renouncing practices derogatory to women's dignity.

56. Domestic Violence Act, 2005

  • The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provides civil remedies against domestic violence.

It supports:

  • Women's dignity.
  • Equality.
  • Protection from abuse.

57. Sexual Harassment at Workplace Act, 2013

The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 supports:

  • Dignity.
  • Equality.
  • Safe working conditions.
  • It is connected with the values expressed in Article 51A(e).

58. Environment Protection Act, 1986

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 provides a broad legal framework for:

  • Pollution control.
  • Environmental protection.
  • It supports Article 51A(g).

59. Environmental Laws Supporting Article 51A(g)

Important laws include:

  • Water Act, 1974.
  • Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
  • Air Act, 1981.
  • Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
  • Forest-conservation legislation.

60. Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984

  • The Act penalises damage to public property.
  • It directly supports the constitutional value under Article 51A(i).
📌 Must-Memorise

Public Property Act, 1984 → Article 51A(i)

61. Right to Education Act, 2009

The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 supports:

  • Article 21A.
  • Article 51A(k).
  • It provides a statutory framework for elementary education.

62. Duty vs Implementing Law

Fundamental Duty:

  • Broad constitutional responsibility.
  • Article 51A itself contains no direct penalty.
  • Guides citizen conduct.

Implementing legislation:

  • Creates specific legal obligations.
  • May prescribe offences or penalties.
  • Is enforceable through legal procedure.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Punishment → Under Implementing Law

Not Directly under Article 51A

63. Fundamental Rights and Duties

Fundamental Rights:

  • Part III.
  • Articles 12–35.
  • Generally justiciable.
  • Enforceable through constitutional courts.

Fundamental Duties:

  • Part IVA.
  • Article 51A.
  • Generally non-justiciable.
  • Civic and constitutional obligations of citizens.

64. Rights Are Not Conditional on Duties

  • A citizen does not lose Fundamental Rights merely because a Fundamental Duty has not been performed.

Any restriction on a Fundamental Right requires:

  • Independent constitutional basis.
  • Legal authority.
  • Fundamental Duties cannot automatically override Fundamental Rights.
📌 Must-Memorise

Failure of Duty ≠ Automatic Loss of Fundamental Rights

65. Duties as Interpretative Aids

Courts may refer to Fundamental Duties when deciding whether legislation or restrictions are:

  • Reasonable.
  • Constitutionally justified.
  • Connected with public interest.

They have been especially relevant in matters concerning:

  • Environment.
  • Education.
  • National symbols.
  • Public discipline.
  • Animal welfare.

66. Speech, Protest and Public Property

Freedom of speech protects:

  • Criticism.
  • Debate.
  • Dissent.
  • Peaceful advocacy.

Peaceful expression does not include:

  • Violence.
  • Arson.
  • Destruction of public property.
  • Article 51A(i) reinforces this distinction.

67. Directive Principles and Duties

Directive Principles:

  • Addressed to the State.
  • Part IV.
  • Articles 36–51.
  • Guide legislation, administration and welfare policy.

Fundamental Duties:

  • Addressed to citizens.
  • Part IVA.
  • Article 51A.
  • Guide civic conduct and social responsibility.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPSP → State

Fundamental Duties → Citizens

68. Shared Environmental Responsibility

  • Article 48A → State must protect environment, forests and wildlife.
  • Article 51A(g) → Citizens must protect the natural environment and living creatures.
  • These provisions create complementary constitutional responsibilities.

69. Shared Educational Responsibility

  • Article 45 → State responsibility concerning early childhood care.
  • Article 21A → State obligation regarding elementary education.
  • Article 51A(k) → Parent or guardian educational responsibility for ages 6–14.

70. Shared Heritage Responsibility

  • Article 49 → State duty to protect nationally important monuments.
  • Article 51A(f) → Citizen duty to preserve India's composite culture.

71. No Direct Article 32 Remedy

  • Fundamental Rights have constitutional remedies such as Article 32.
  • Fundamental Duties do not have an equivalent direct enforcement mechanism.
  • A person generally cannot approach the Supreme Court solely to demand punishment of another person for failure to perform a Fundamental Duty.

72. Courts Cannot Create Crimes from Duties

  • Courts cannot treat Article 51A alone as a criminal law.

Punishment requires:

  • Valid legislation.
  • Defined offence.
  • Prescribed penalty.
  • Due process.
  • Courts may nevertheless use duties in constitutional interpretation.

73. Fundamental Duties and PIL

A Public Interest Litigation may involve Fundamental Duties together with:

  • Article 21.
  • Statutory obligations.
  • Directive Principles.
  • Public-trust principles.
  • Fundamental Duty usually does not operate as the sole enforceable right.

74. State Responsibilities Continue

  • Citizen duties do not release governments from their own constitutional obligations.

Effective civic responsibility also requires:

  • Public awareness.
  • Education.
  • Institutional example.
  • Transparent government.
  • Civic participation.

75. Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala, 1986

  • The case concerned the National Anthem and freedom of conscience.
  • Students respectfully stood during the National Anthem but did not sing because of sincere religious belief.

The Supreme Court protected their constitutional freedom where:

  • No disrespect was shown.
  • No disturbance was caused.
  • The decision demonstrates that Fundamental Duties must be harmonised with Fundamental Rights.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bijoe Emmanuel → 1986 → National Anthem + Freedom of Conscience

76. M.C. Mehta Environmental Cases

The Supreme Court used constitutional provisions including:

  • Article 21.
  • Article 48A.
  • Article 51A(g).
  • Environmental protection, awareness and education were treated as shared constitutional concerns.
📌 Must-Memorise

M.C. Mehta → Environment → 21 + 48A + 51A(g)

77. Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra Case

  • The Court dealt with ecological damage caused by mining.

78. Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal, 1987

  • The Supreme Court emphasised that courts should keep environmental constitutional provisions in mind when deciding ecological matters.
  • Articles 48A and 51A(g) received particular attention.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sachidanand Pandey → 1987 → 48A + 51A(g)

79. AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS, 2001

  • The Supreme Court emphasised the constitutional importance of Fundamental Duties.

It connected Article 51A(j) with:

  • Excellence.

  • National development.
  • Constitutional interpretation.
📌 Must-Memorise

AIIMS Students' Union → 2001 → Article 51A(j)

80. Aruna Roy v. Union of India, 2002

  • The Supreme Court considered questions relating to value education.

It distinguished:

81. Union of India v. Naveen Jindal, 2004

  • The case dealt with the right to fly the National Flag.

The right remains subject to:

  • National-honour requirements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Naveen Jindal → 2004 → Right to Fly National Flag

82. Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja, 2014

The Supreme Court connected:

  • Animal welfare.

with Article 51A(g).

📌 Must-Memorise

A. Nagaraja → 2014 → Compassion for Living Creatures → 51A(g)

83. Common Judicial Principle

The important cases establish that Fundamental Duties:

  • Cannot ordinarily override Fundamental Rights.
  • Can guide constitutional interpretation.
  • Can support valid legislation.
  • Can strengthen public-interest obligations.
  • Must operate consistently with constitutional liberty.

  • Inserted Part IVA.
  • Inserted Article 51A.
  • Added ten duties.

  • Inserted Article 21A.
  • Modified Article 45.
  • Added Article 51A(k).
  • Increased duties from 10 to 11.

Were Fundamental Duties part of the original Constitution? → No.

When were Fundamental Duties added? → 1976.

Which Committee recommended their constitutional inclusion? → Swaran Singh Committee.

In which year was the Swaran Singh Committee associated with this recommendation? → 1976.

Which Constitutional Amendment inserted Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

Which Part was inserted? → Part IVA.

Which Article contains Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A.

How many Articles are contained in Part IVA? → One, Article 51A.

How many duties were originally added? → Ten.

How many duties are there now? → Eleven.

Which Amendment added the eleventh duty? → 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.

Which duty was added by the 86th Amendment? → Article 51A(k).

What does Article 51A(k) require? → Parent or guardian must provide educational opportunity to a child or ward aged 6–14 years.

Which Committee examined existing laws giving effect to Fundamental Duties? → J.S. Verma Committee.

When was the J.S. Verma Committee associated with this review? → 1998.

What is the basic difference between Swaran Singh and Verma Committees? → Swaran Singh recommended constitutional inclusion; Verma examined implementation through existing laws.

To whom do Fundamental Duties apply? → Citizens of India.

Do Fundamental Duties constitutionally apply to foreigners? → No.

Do they apply to companies as citizens? → No.

Are Fundamental Duties generally justiciable? → No.

Does Article 51A itself prescribe punishment? → No.

Can Parliament or State Legislatures enact laws implementing duties? → Yes, where constitutionally competent.

Can such laws provide penalties? → Yes.

Is punishment imposed directly under Article 51A? → No; it arises under implementing legislation.

Which duty requires respect for Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem? → Article 51A(a).

Which duty refers to noble ideals of the freedom struggle? → Article 51A(b).

Which duty concerns sovereignty, unity and integrity? → Article 51A(c).

Which duty concerns defence of the country? → Article 51A(d).

Does Article 51A(d) itself create universal compulsory military service? → No.

Which duty promotes harmony and common brotherhood? → Article 51A(e).

Which duty also requires renouncing practices derogatory to women's dignity? → Article 51A(e).

Which duty concerns preservation of India's composite culture? → Article 51A(f).

Which duty concerns the natural environment? → Article 51A(g).

Which duty requires compassion for living creatures? → Article 51A(g).

Which duty concerns scientific temper? → Article 51A(h).

What four ideas are contained in Article 51A(h)? → Scientific temper, humanism, spirit of inquiry and reform.

Which duty concerns public property? → Article 51A(i).

Which duty asks citizens to abjure violence? → Article 51A(i).

Which duty concerns excellence? → Article 51A(j).

Which duty concerns education of children aged 6–14? → Article 51A(k).

Which is the only Fundamental Duty specifically directed at parents or guardians? → Article 51A(k).

Which Article places environmental responsibility on the State? → Article 48A.

Which Article places environmental responsibility on citizens? → Article 51A(g).

Which Article provides the Fundamental Right to elementary education? → Article 21A.

Which Article places related responsibility on parents or guardians? → Article 51A(k).

Which Article places heritage responsibility on the State? → Article 49.

Which duty asks citizens to preserve composite culture? → Article 51A(f).

Which Act is strongly associated with respect for the National Flag and Anthem? → Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.

Which Code regulates display and use of the National Flag? → Flag Code of India, 2002.

Which Act restricts improper use of specified national emblems and official names? → Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950.

Which Act is associated with protection of sovereignty and integrity? → Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.

Which Act supports constitutional protection against untouchability? → Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.

Which Act protects SCs and STs from specified atrocities? → SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

Which law supports women's dignity in relation to dowry? → Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.

Which law provides remedies against domestic violence? → Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

Which law addresses workplace sexual harassment? → Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013.

Which major Act supports Article 51A(g)? → Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

Name other environmental laws mentioned in the reference. → Water Act, 1974; Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; Air Act, 1981; forest-conservation legislation.

Which Act protects public property? → Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984.

Which Act supports Article 21A and Article 51A(k)? → Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009.

Can a citizen lose Fundamental Rights merely for failing to perform a Fundamental Duty? → No.

Can Fundamental Duties override Fundamental Rights automatically? → No.

Can courts use Duties while interpreting laws? → Yes.

Can a Fundamental Duty support reasonable restrictions where a valid constitutional and legal basis exists? → Yes.

Which case dealt with National Anthem and freedom of conscience? → Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala, 1986.

What did Bijoe Emmanuel establish? → Respectful conduct and sincere freedom of conscience must be harmonised; duties do not automatically override Fundamental Rights.

Which cases connected environmental protection with Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g)? → M.C. Mehta environmental cases.

Which case dealt with ecological damage caused by mining? → Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

Which 1987 case emphasised Articles 48A and 51A(g)? → Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal.

Which case is associated with Article 51A(j) and excellence? → AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS, 2001.

Which case dealt with value education? → Aruna Roy v. Union of India, 2002.

Which case recognised flying the National Flag with dignity as protected expression subject to regulation? → Union of India v. Naveen Jindal, 2004.

Which case connected compassion for living creatures with Article 51A(g)? → Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja, 2014.

What is the key difference between DPSP and Fundamental Duties? → DPSPs are addressed to the State; Fundamental Duties are addressed to citizens.

Which Part contains DPSP? → Part IV.

Which Part contains Fundamental Duties? → Part IVA.

Are both generally non-justiciable? → Yes.

What is the easiest way to remember the amendment history? → 42nd Amendment = first 10 duties; 86th Amendment = 11th educational duty.
